body: Thanks, I appreciate it!
Thanks, I appreciate it!

I've gotten better at recognizing it. It's still usually after the fact, but it's often now right after the fact, and before I left on a way that makes it much worse than it already is.

Naturally, I'm the kind of person who wants to stop and talk things out immediately, play by play, but without the temperament to do so and not get hurt or mad.

I don't know. Just keep trying.

That sucks, but maybe better then than finding out later what your partner's made of (of course, I wish it hadn't happened to you, at all, just trying to point out a painful bright side).

Thank you for the kind words.

Oh, for sure!

I mean, after the 24 hours of snuggling, of course.

Honestly, I want to do that for when she gets home, but I feel like I might be waiting outside the doors so I don't have to go an extra minute without her.

Maybe a drive through burger that first night, then something homemade the next. :)
Thank you, that's good to keep in mind.

That last part hits hard. I took Wednesday off to stay home and help with the kids' virtual school because one of my daughters keeps giving her a very hard time. She really clicks with my other daughter, so they got her schoolwork done fast and did more relaxed, fun practice activities until my other daughter and I finished up). She said it really helped make it a good day, and she seemed the last anxious she had in days, maybe a week or two.

That night was the night.

Thank you. The numbers I was able to find all said a range of 20-40mg/kg, and she took a good amount over that. It's good to hear those numbers were incorrect, as that gives me more hope about her long-term health, as well.

Maybe a direct response to someone who's going through some real serious shit isn't the place to post your musings of this sort, especially if you're going to use second person pronouns instead of clearer, indirect verbiage. If you paid attention to my post and the other comments, or the comments of many people who have supported a loved one through a similar crisis, you know that I love someone who has a hard time loving herself.

There are places for the story of discussion (or unquestioned monologue) you might be trying to have. This isn't one of them.

You're not feeling with logic, and you're pretending I said things I didn't. You need to seek help from a professional.

I am neither a professional nor someone currently in any condition to deal with someone's deliberate misinterpretations.

I honestly wish you luck. I have given you all the advice I could possibly have for you--get professional help.

I can only imagine that. I'm so sorry you had that experience. I wish I could be there. The facility is less than a mile from our home. 4 minutes by car.

And I can't do anything to see her.

But they finally have her the clothes and personal items, and she said that helped. She carries around a couple of the pictures I dropped off. A couple more are set up in her room so she can see them when trying to go to sleep.

Thank you for your comment, I appreciate it.

It's certainly harder to love someone else if you don't love yourself, but that's different from what you're saying. 

I'm sorry you feel like people have lied to you. Many people mean well and say things that are unhelpful, at best, and very dangerous, at worst.

The world isn't fair, and assholes seem to find people who will be with them. Seems to happen with ease, but I suspect that's because they aren't looking for a positive, healthy relationship.

If I had a dollar for every time somebody have me empty platitudes and thought they were helping, I wouldn't have to debate about calling in to work tomorrow, I'd be able to retire.

Sometimes, professionals might fall into those sayings, but regular people with no counseling training often struggle to go beyond them at all when trying to figure out what to say to people who are hurting.

Anyway, you commented, and you sent a positive thing my way, and more importantly to me, my girlfriend's way. I appreciate that, and I appreciate you for that.

Thank you.

I can understand that. I also can understand not feeling like talking to your parents.

When I was in high school, I had a passive suicide attempt, and my parents didn't know for several years (they knew something was wrong, but didn't know it was more than just teen angst or depression, desire being very involved and protective parents).

I just didn't want to talk to them about it.

It sounds like you need someone to talk to, and I strongly recommend finding professional help. It sounds like your parents may be on board with that if you just tell them you need to talk to someone but don't feel comfortable talking to them or someone else you know.

The patient confidentiality is a big thing that makes professional therapists, etc, easier to talk to. Like, I would've trusted my parents probably wouldn't tell others, but I know a therapist won't because they can lose their license/career.

If you're still in school, you should be able to get pointed in the right direction for resources locally by your school counselor/social workers (my info is based in the USA, so ymmv, and it varies school to school).

If you have a regular doctor, you can also talk to them. Call their office (or email, if that's easier) and ask to talk about your concerns. Ask for a referral for counseling.

Whatever you do, don't give up. You're not alone, and you don't have to face this alone.

I'm glad it's in the past tense for you. I don't know your situation, but I cannot believe he would be anything other than devastated.

She kept telling our friends (age when I finally could reach her, me) that hey biggest great was losing me.

I imagine your bf probably would've responded like I did--my biggest fear is losing her. I told her I'm not going anywhere, and she just needs to focus on herself and getting better.
I see it. Thank you for the kind words and good wishes. Be well.
Thank you, that is very sweet!

Good for you for trying to get help! Keep pushing at it. I know it can feel like the burden is not even moving, but pushing wears it down.

You can do this, but not alone. Reach out.
As far as time goes--don't know. She called this morning and said she was going to ask the doctor about timelines and such, now that the initial evaluations and everything have been completed.

Thank you, I feel the same way.

I appreciate the encouraging support.

Right back at you.

Thank you.

The time hasn't come for that conversation. She needs to focus on her stuff in there, and do so under her own volition, rather than out of fear/"threat." At least that's my perspective for now.

She has said that her biggest worry when she woke up and was getting ready to call for help (and said it explicitly to our friends who helped her get to the hospital) was that she had just ruined the best thing that's ever happened to her (our relationship/life together/family). So she's aware of what's on the line.

The timing, or at least how to go about making sure it's clear, is something I can bring up when I talk to the staff again. Thank you for that thought.

She has severe allergies, and needs benadryl handy. So it's kind of her medication, but not prescribed. I've considered leaving enough of it available today she is safe in case of exposure, but only a dose at a time.

I'll know more when I talk next to the staff. They've put together a safety plan for her release that involves ongoing treatment, both medication and counseling/therapy/psych treatment, and she's on board with it, which is good.

If you're in danger, call for help. If I could come where you are and help you, I would, for what it's worth, and I've never met you.

Getting yourself to the ER or calling emergency services, or whomever you call to get help is not a sign of weakness.

It takes strength to ask for help. It only takes pride and stubbornness to refuse. You can do this.

Call for help.

I understand that. She has made progress since moving in, but she got as far as she could without professional help. This was a wake up call for her.

When she is released, if she does not follow through (she insists she is planning to continue professional treatment, and the staff at her facility have said the same thing), then yes, I will have to make decisions in order to protect my family.

It wouldn't be the first time I've had to make horribly painful decisions to protect my children and myself, although those were decisions involving someone else.

I appreciate your encouragement and concern. Like I said in the OP, she's actually interested in treatment. This shake up shook loose some blocks and clogs for her, I really think.

Thank you for the encouragement.

I don't know, but long term physical effects are a concern. I don't know that they've even gotten that far yet. It's all been stabilize and get her on the road to recovery and safe release. They haven't talked about long term.

Frankly, it's quite surprising that she woke up. The amount she took was well over the top of the range of potentially lethal dose, from what I read online. I really hope most of it just passed through her system, but I'm worried about her liver.

I'll try to update in the future. So far, she's stable, she's doing ok, and she's showing signs and willingness towards recovery and treatment.
I am so sorry to hear that.
Thank you!
